strengths: Addresses a real and important problem: SBI on computationally expensive simulators, where simulation budget is the primary bottleneck; the proposed MF-NPE is well-motivated and practically relevant across scientific domains.

Clear and honest presentation: the method (pre-training on low-fidelity simulations via transfer learning, extended to MF-TSNPE and an active-learning variant A-MF-TSNPE) is well described with complete algorithms and implementation details (Appendices A-F), supporting reproducibility.

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation across three tasks spanning increasing difficulty: an OU process with ground-truth posterior (C2ST), a multicompartmental neuron model, and a challenging 24-parameter spiking network with plastic synapses; includes multiple fidelity ratios, multiple low-fidelity dataset sizes, dimensionality-mismatch settings, posterior predictive checks, and simulation-based calibration.

Consistent empirical evidence that MF-NPE matches NPE performance with up to two orders of magnitude fewer high-fidelity simulations (e.g., Table 1, Fig. 10), and the demonstrated use of a mean-field model as a low-fidelity surrogate for a spiking network is a genuinely useful demonstration for practitioners.

Good related-work positioning, including a thoughtful discussion of connections to model misspecification (e.g., ROPE) and limitations (similarity of fidelities, inherited NPE/TSNPE limitations, bias risk of the acquisition function).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core method is essentially warm-starting a normalizing flow pre-trained on low-fidelity data, plus combining it with existing TSNPE and an existing ensemble-variance acquisition function; no new theory or analysis of when/why the transfer succeeds, and the method is a fairly straightforward composition of known components.

Baselines are incomplete: comparison is only against NPE/TSNPE; no comparison against other likelihood-free multifidelity approaches (e.g., multifidelity ABC/SMC-ABC or sequential tempered MCMC variants cited in related work) or against simpler alternatives such as training a surrogate/emulator of the high-fidelity simulator and running NPE on it, or simply mixing LF and HF data in a single training set with importance weighting.

Cost accounting is not fully fair: MF-NPE uses 10^4-10^5 low-fidelity simulations for pre-training; while c_L << c, the total compute (including LF simulation and pre-training cost) is not systematically compared across methods, so the 'two orders of magnitude fewer simulations' claim refers only to high-fidelity simulations.

The active-learning variant A-MF-TSNPE yields only minor improvements over MF-TSNPE despite substantially higher cost (ensembles, extra hyperparameters), and its potential to bias the proposal is acknowledged but not theoretically resolved, weakening this claimed contribution.

Generality of the conclusions is constrained: in the OU task the low-fidelity model is a drastic simplification chosen by the authors; there is no systematic study of how performance degrades as the low-fidelity model becomes less similar to the high-fidelity model, which is central to when the method is useful.

No hyperparameter sensitivity analysis or ablation of key choices (e.g., number of pre-training epochs, early stopping criterion, effect of logit transforms, ensemble size for the acquisition function).

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and well-motivated problem: reducing the simulation budget of SBI for expensive high-fidelity simulators, which affects many scientific domains.

The proposed MF-NPE method is clearly described, easy to reproduce (Algorithm 1, hyperparameter details in Appendix A), and built on standard, well-tested components (neural spline flows, TSNPE, the sbi toolkit).

The empirical evaluation uses appropriate metrics (C2ST when ground truth is available, NLTP otherwise), multiple network initializations with confidence intervals, and standard validation tools (posterior predictive checks, simulation-based calibration).

The demonstration on two genuinely expensive neuroscience simulators (multicompartmental L5PC neuron, recurrent spiking network with plasticity) gives the claims practical relevance, and gains of up to two orders of magnitude in high-fidelity simulations are plausibly supported by the experiments.
Honest discussion of limitations, including the reliance on low/high-fidelity similarity and the modest benefit of the active learning component.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. The core contribution amounts to pre-training a density estimator on low-fidelity simulations and fine-tuning on high-fidelity ones — a straightforward application of standard transfer learning. The active learning extension is a straightforward variance-acquisition ensemble scheme adapted from prior work and yields only 'minor improvements' by the authors' own admission. There is no theoretical analysis of when or why the approach helps, nor any principled treatment of the bias introduced by the acquisition function (the authors explicitly sidestep it and rely on an empirical hypothesis).

The baseline comparison is too weak. The method is only compared to vanilla NPE and TSNPE. Missing baselines include: (i) simply fine-tuning on generic or mixed data, (ii) other likelihood-free multifidelity approaches cited in the related work (Prescott & Baker, Warne et al.), (iii) surrogate/emulator-based pipelines that are the standard alternative in multifidelity UQ, and (iv) more recent SBI methods (e.g., diffusion-based estimators the authors themselves cite as future work). Without these, the evidence that the proposed scheme is the right way to use low-fidelity data is incomplete.

Simulation budget accounting is not rigorous. The headline claim of 'two orders of magnitude fewer high-fidelity simulations' ignores the low-fidelity budget, which is substantial (10^4–10^5 pre-training samples) and requires constructing a bespoke low-fidelity model per task by domain experts. A compute- or wall-clock-normalized comparison (including the cost of designing and validating the low-fidelity model) would substantially temper the claimed efficiency gains, and is not provided.

The OU task, where C2ST is computed, has a tractable likelihood and very cheap low/high-fidelity models, so it primarily serves as a sanity check; the real evidence rests on only two neuroscience tasks from the same research ecosystem (same group's simulators, priors taken from prior works of the same lab). Generalization to other scientific domains is asserted but not demonstrated.

Some experimental details are underspecified or inconsistent: the injection current parameters differ between main text (0.3 nA noisy current) and appendix (0.55 mV step current); the effect of the low-fidelity budget saturates between 10^4 and 10^5 without explanation; posterior leakage mitigations (logit transforms) were needed for baselines, raising questions about whether baselines were tuned as carefully as the proposed method.

The claimed contribution of 'two active learning schemes' overstates the delta: A-MF-TSNPE differs from MF-TSNPE only by adding an ensemble-based acquisition to the proposal and brings negligible gains at substantially higher cost, as the authors concede.

strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem in simulation-based inference (SBI): reducing the simulation budget of expensive high-fidelity simulators, which is highly relevant across scientific domains.

The proposed MF-NPE method is simple, well-motivated (transfer learning from low- to high-fidelity density estimators), and clearly described, including extension to sequential training (MF-TSNPE) and an active learning variant (A-MF-TSNPE) with full algorithms provided.

Solid empirical evaluation across three tasks of increasing realism and dimensionality (OU process with ground truth, a multicompartmental neuron model, and a 24-parameter spiking network with mean-field low-fidelity model), with appropriate metrics (C2ST when ground truth is available, NLTP otherwise), simulation-based calibration checks, posterior predictive checks, and multiple network initializations with confidence intervals.

Demonstrated sample-efficiency gains (e.g., comparable performance to NPE with up to two orders of magnitude fewer high-fidelity simulations) and a concrete real-world result (30% increase in plausible posterior samples on the spiking network task).

Honest discussion of limitations: dependence on similarity between fidelities, inherited scalability limitations of NPE/TSNPE, the modest gains and high cost of the ensemble-based acquisition function, and the uncorrected potential bias from active proposals.

Clear positioning within related work (multifidelity inference, transfer learning for simulators, model misspecification/ROPE), and a codebase built on standard toolkits (sbi, Zuko), supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core contribution is straightforward warm-starting/fine-tuning of a neural density estimator trained on low-fidelity data, which is a natural application of transfer learning. The authors' claim that transfer learning for SBI 'has not been realized yet' is somewhat overstated given related work on transfer learning for simulators and emulator-based pretraining (e.g., Lueckmann et al., 2019).

Evaluation cost accounting is incomplete: the headline claim of 'two orders of magnitude fewer high-fidelity simulations' ignores the cost of generating 10^4–10^5 low-fidelity simulations and the additional training/ensemble overhead, so total wall-clock or computational savings are not rigorously quantified.

Baselines are limited to NPE and TSNPE; no empirical comparison to other likelihood-free multifidelity approaches (e.g., multifidelity ABC/SMC-ABC of Prescott & Baker) or to surrogate/emulator-based alternatives, beyond a qualitative argument that they do not scale.

The active learning variant (A-MF-TSNPE) yields only 'minor improvements' over MF-TSNPE while being substantially more expensive and introducing an acknowledged, uncorrected proposal bias; its contribution as a second 'core contribution' is therefore weak and the bias-accuracy tradeoff is not quantified.

All real-world tasks are from computational neuroscience, largely on setups closely related to the authors' own prior work; results on tasks from other scientific domains would strengthen generality claims.

Several figures/tables (e.g., Fig. 3, Table 1) show only a subset of conditions in the main text, and some quantitative gains at the largest simulation budgets become small, making the practical benefit at high budgets less clear.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and well-motivated problem: reducing simulation cost in SBI when high-fidelity simulators are expensive and a low-fidelity simulator is available from domain expertise.

Method is simple, general, and well-integrated: transfer learning is applied consistently to both amortized NPE and sequential TSNPE, extended with a variance-based acquisition function (A-MF-TSNPE), and supports multiple fidelity levels and mismatched parameter dimensionalities (dummy-variable trick).

Unusually broad and careful empirical evaluation: four benchmark tasks plus two realistic, expensive neuroscience simulators (L5PC multicompartment neuron; 24-parameter spiking network with mean-field low-fidelity model), with standard SBI metrics (C2ST, MMD, NLTP, NRMSE), SBC calibration checks, posterior predictive checks, and 10+ network initializations with confidence intervals.

Honest cost accounting (Appendix K) distinguishes simulation cost from training cost, clarifying when the approach is beneficial; also compares to MF-ABC and discusses fair caveats regarding its hyperparameters.
Goes beyond a benchmark score with an empirical study of *when* transfer helps (mutual information and representational coherence, Appendix B), which adds scientific value.
Good limitations and future-work discussion; acknowledges concurrent MF-SBI efforts (Thiele et al., Hikida et al., Saoulis et al.) and positions against ABC-based and surrogate-based alternatives.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is modest: the core algorithm is standard pretraining/fine-tuning of a normalizing flow combined with existing TSNPE and ensemble-based acquisition; several concurrent works (Thiele et al. 2025, Saoulis et al. 2025) do very similar things, and the paper does not empirically compare against any of them, making it hard to assess relative merit within the emerging MF-SBI landscape.

Benchmark tasks are low-dimensional (2-5 parameters; the hardest real task has 24), whereas scalability to high-dimensional parameter spaces is exactly where NPE/TSNPE struggle; the paper itself admits this limitation but the headline claim of 'orders of magnitude' efficiency gains is not tested in a regime where it matters most.

Gains from the active-learning variant A-MF-TSNPE are inconsistent (improves only the OU task, 'did not show significant improvements' on SLCP/SIR) and come with substantial training-cost overhead, weakening one of the three claimed contributions.

No theoretical analysis: the paper offers only a trivial convergence restatement (Appendix C) of standard NPE; the transfer-learning question is addressed purely empirically on a single controlled OU2 experiment with MINE-estimated mutual information, which is a noisy estimator and limited evidence for a general claim.

The assumption of negligible low-fidelity cost is not always realistic; only one real task (spiking network) has an extreme cost ratio, while the L5PC task has HF/LF cost ratio of only ~4x, where the end-to-end gains are much less dramatic (4-5x total cost reduction).

Code and data are only promised 'upon publication', which limits reproducibility assessment at review time; the multilevel benchmark the authors themselves call for is not released as a concrete resource.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem—reducing the simulation cost of SBI for expensive simulators—which is relevant across scientific domains.

The evaluation is relatively broad: four benchmark tasks plus two realistic, computationally expensive neuroscience simulators, with multiple metrics (C2ST, MMD, NLTP, NRMSE), simulation-based calibration, posterior predictive checks, and an explicit wall-clock cost analysis (Appendix K).
The empirical investigation of when pre-training helps (mutual information and representational coherence, Appendix B) is a nice addition beyond just reporting benchmark wins.
The method is simple and well-documented: full training details, algorithm pseudocode, hyperparameters, and reproducibility statement are provided, and code is promised to be released.
The limitations section is candid, acknowledging dependence on low/high-fidelity similarity, inherited NPE/TSNPE limitations, and the ensemble cost of A-MF-TSNPE.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core contribution is standard fine-tuning/pre-training of a neural density estimator from low- to high-fidelity simulations, a direct adaptation of well-known transfer learning to existing NPE/TSNPE pipelines. The paper itself acknowledges closely concurrent works (Thiele et al., 2025; Hikida et al., 2025; Saoulis et al., 2025) that do essentially related things (multi-fidelity SBI via distillation, multilevel Monte Carlo for SBI, transfer learning for SBI), yet does not empirically compare against any of them—only against the much weaker MF-ABC baseline.

No comparison to the most natural baselines in the 'simulation-efficient SBI' space (e.g., learned surrogate simulators, Bayesian neural network posteriors, signature-based ratio estimation) that the related-work section itself surveys; this makes it hard to assess whether multifidelity transfer is actually the best way to spend the same total compute.

The 'up to two orders of magnitude fewer simulations' claim from the abstract is not fully supported when total computational cost is considered: Appendix K shows only 4-5x total cost reduction for the L5PC task, and the headline gains rely on assuming low-fidelity simulations are essentially free, an assumption the authors themselves flag as a limitation and defer to future work.

No theory or analysis of when/why the approach works beyond a purely empirical study; the convergence 'proof' in Appendix C is a textbook KL-divergence identity for standard NPE, not specific to the multifidelity method, and does not address the transfer learning setting at all.

Results are mixed: the A-MF-TSNPE variant shows 'no significant improvements' on SLCP and SIR, and MF-NPE gains diminish or vanish at higher simulation budgets (e.g., no improvement between 10^4 and 10^5 low-fidelity samples), suggesting the benefits are confined to specific regimes; the spiking network task only compares against NPE without sequential variants and relies on NLTP without ground-truth posteriors.

The acquisition-function variant introduces a known bias into the proposal distribution that is 'argued away' (Appendix M.2) rather than corrected or empirically quantified, which raises soundness concerns about posterior accuracy of A-MF-TSNPE.

The 'when does pre-training help' analysis (Appendix B) is restricted to a single synthetic OU task with controlled perturbations and uses MINE-based estimates of mutual information, whose reliability at these scales is questionable; generalization of the two-factor hypothesis to real tasks is not demonstrated.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: reducing the simulation cost of NPE for expensive simulators via multifidelity pre-training is practically relevant across scientific domains.

The method is simple, well-specified, and complete: full pseudocode for MF-NPE, MF-TSNPE, and A-MF-TSNPE (Algorithms 1-4), including a generalization to more than two fidelity levels and to mismatched parameter spaces (dummy variables for HF-exclusive parameters).

Comprehensive evaluation: four benchmark tasks (including a new OU multifidelity task with tractable likelihood and a high-dimensional image task) plus two genuinely expensive, realistic neuroscience simulators, with standard SBI metrics (C2ST, MMD, NLTP, NRMSE), simulation-based calibration, posterior predictive checks, and 10-30 observations with multiple network seeds.
Cost analysis (Appendix K) goes beyond simulation counts to wall-clock training vs. simulation costs, honestly identifying when the method pays off (L5PC and spiking network) and when it does not.

The empirical study of when pre-training helps (Appendix B, mutual information and representational coherence) and of joint pre-training alternatives (Appendix H.3) adds useful insight beyond the method itself.
Honest limitations section, discussion of concurrent work (Thiele et al., Saoulis et al., Hikida et al.), and comparison against MF-ABC including a hyperparameter sweep for the baseline.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core method is straightforward fine-tuning/weight initialization of an NSF pretrained on low-fidelity data, applied to NPE/TSNPE. Concurrent works (Thiele et al. 2025, Saoulis et al. 2025, Hikida et al. 2025) address closely related ideas; there is no head-to-head empirical comparison against any of these multifidelity SBI alternatives, which weakens the claim of state-of-the-art efficiency.

The benchmark tasks assume the low-fidelity simulator is nearly free, and the amortized benchmarks pretrain on 10^4-10^5 low-fidelity simulations. Although the neuroscience tasks do account for total cost, the headline claim of 'up to two orders of magnitude fewer high-fidelity simulations' could be misleading if low-fidelity costs were non-negligible; the total-budget accounting is deferred to only two tasks.

A-MF-TSNPE, the advertised algorithmic contribution beyond transfer, shows no significant improvement on SLCP and SIR (as the authors admit), so its practical value rests on limited evidence (OU process, L5PC). The acknowledged bias of the acquisition function on the proposal is handled only by an informal argument (B = 0.2M) without analysis of the resulting posterior bias.

No comparison against other simulation-efficiency baselines from the single-fidelity literature the paper itself discusses (e.g., Bayesian neural networks under small budgets (Delaunay et al. 2024), signature-based ratio estimation (Dyer et al. 2022)), so the gains are only benchmarked against vanilla NPE/TSNPE and MF-ABC.

The theoretical analysis is minimal (standard NPE loss-as-KL derivation in Appendix C); the transfer-learning question is left to qualitative empirical observations, so the conditions under which the method fails remain poorly characterized.

Some sensitivity to LF model quality and parameter-space mismatch is reported (OU3/OU4 degradation), but guidance on when pre-training helps versus hurts in practice is only partially addressed; claims in the abstract are somewhat stronger than the mixed per-task evidence (e.g., modest gains on SLCP/SIR at high budgets).
